name: Empowering Individual Decision-Making
what: This subtopic covers how independence develops through the self-determination theory and its three psychological needs (autonomy, competence, and relatedness), and how anti-conformity can be encouraged through reactance, individuation, the desire to promote change, and social support.
why: Understanding the psychological conditions that allow individuals to act on their own values rather than group pressure is important for evaluating individual behaviour in real-world contexts and for recognising how people can resist harmful social influences.

items.title: I can define independence and explain how it differs from simply ignoring social norms
items.what: Independence means being free from the control or influence of others when making decisions, with choices driven by personal beliefs and intrinsic motivation rather than external pressure. An independent person may still choose behaviours that align with group norms, but the driver of that choice is internal.
items.why: Independence is often confused with deliberate rule-breaking, but a truly independent person acts authentically regardless of whether that action happens to match or contradict group expectations.
items.example: A student who dresses in a way considered unfashionable, simply because they prefer that style, is demonstrating independence. A student who deliberately wears something unfashionable to annoy others is displaying anti-conformity rather than independence.

items.title: I can distinguish between intrinsic and extrinsic motivation and link intrinsic motivation to self-determination
items.what: Extrinsic motivation involves engaging in behaviours for external rewards such as money, praise, or avoiding negative judgment. Intrinsic motivation involves engaging in behaviours for internal rewards such as personal growth, curiosity, or satisfaction. Self-determination, and therefore independence, is primarily driven by intrinsic motivation.
items.why: People who are primarily extrinsically motivated remain dependent on others to define what is worth doing, making them more susceptible to social pressure. Shifting toward intrinsic motivation is therefore central to developing independence.
items.example: A student who studies psychology because they find human behaviour genuinely fascinating is intrinsically motivated. A student who studies it only to please their parents is extrinsically motivated and may be more likely to change their choices if parental expectations shift.

items.title: I can name and define the three basic psychological needs in self-determination theory
items.what: The self-determination theory, developed by Ryan and Deci, identifies three needs that must all be met for full independence: autonomy (acting based on personal choice and intrinsic motivation), competence (having the skills to carry out meaningful actions), and relatedness (feeling a genuine sense of belonging and connection to others).
items.why: Because all three needs must be fulfilled for true independence to develop, identifying which need is unmet in a given scenario allows a precise explanation of why someone is not acting independently.
items.example: Cody feels connected to friends (relatedness met) and believes he can choose his own path (autonomy met), but doubts his academic abilities (competence not met). This unfulfilled need prevents him from fully acting on his own values without being swayed by others' opinions.

items.title: I can explain how each of the three self-determination needs specifically promotes independent decision-making in a group context
items.what: Autonomy supports independent decision-making by increasing belief that one's individual actions are meaningful. Competence reduces susceptibility to social influence by increasing confidence in one's own judgment. Relatedness supports independence when peers are supportive rather than controlling, removing the fear of social rejection.
items.why: These mechanisms explain how group settings can either suppress or support independence, and provide a framework for understanding why some people resist social pressure more effectively than others.
items.example: A skilled debater (competence met) who believes their vote counts (autonomy met) and whose family supports their choices (relatedness met) is more likely to vote according to their own research than to match the opinions of a social group.

items.title: I can define anti-conformity and explain why it must be deliberate to qualify as anti-conformity
items.what: Anti-conformity is a deliberate refusal to comply with social norms or standards, involving both active resistance to the expectations of others and the purposeful expression of attitudes or behaviours that challenge those norms. Non-conformity that is accidental, such as a tourist unknowingly breaking a local custom, does not qualify.
items.why: The deliberate nature of anti-conformity is what distinguishes it psychologically: research by Seery et al. found that intentional deviation from group opinion produces a physiological 'challenge' state, whereas unintentional deviation produces a 'threat' state.
items.example: A model who deliberately posts unfiltered photos on Instagram to challenge unrealistic beauty standards is engaging in anti-conformity. A person who simply never learned that filters were expected is not, because there is no deliberate refusal.

items.title: I can identify and explain four factors that encourage anti-conformity
items.what: Four factors encourage anti-conformity: the desire to promote change (a belief that current norms are unjust), reactance (motivational resistance triggered when personal freedom is threatened), individuation (being visible and identifiable within a group, increasing felt responsibility), and social support (having at least one other person who shares your position).
items.why: These factors either provide the motivation to act against norms or weaken the forces that make conformity feel necessary. Understanding them allows analysis of real-world cases where individuals resist group pressure.
items.example: A teenager who wants to attend a school climate strike during class hours is more likely to do so if one friend joins them (social support) and if a teacher uses language like 'you must stay in school' (reactance). Either factor alone increases the likelihood of anti-conformist action.

items.title: I can explain how anti-conformity and independence relate to each other and why an independent person does not always display anti-conformity
items.what: Independence involves making decisions free from external influence, while anti-conformity involves deliberately opposing social norms. An independent person acts based on their own values, which may sometimes align with group norms, meaning no anti-conformity is required or desired.
items.why: Conflating independence with anti-conformity leads to the incorrect assumption that an independent person must always behave unusually. A person can be fully independent and still choose to follow common social practices, simply because those practices reflect their genuine preferences.
items.example: An independent person who genuinely enjoys shaking hands when meeting new people will do so in a job interview because it reflects their preference, not because they fear being judged. They are conforming to a social norm, but from a place of independence, not social pressure.

items.title: I can define a deviant subgroup and explain how social support from one can empower individual decision-making
items.what: A deviant subgroup is a group that holds values and norms outside the dominant social norms of society. Having even one additional supporter who shares a dissenting view can significantly increase an individual's willingness to act on that view, by reducing the perceived unanimity of the majority and weakening groupthink.
items.why: Research extending Asch's findings shows that unanimity is a critical driver of conformity: break the unanimity and conformity drops sharply. A deviant subgroup, even a small one, provides this interruption, making individual decision-making more achievable.
items.example: In Asch's experiment, introducing a single confederate who gave the correct answer caused conformity rates to drop markedly, demonstrating that the presence of even one supporter reduces the pressure to match the majority's position.
